title: The History of Programming
passages: Long before electricity, a brilliant ENGLISH mathematician named Ada Lovelace imagined the future. Working alongside the inventor Charles Babbage, she studied his designs for the Analytical Engine — a mechanical computing MACHINE that was never fully built. In 1843, Ada published a set of notes containing what is now recognised as the first algorithm ever WRITTEN to be carried out by a machine, making her the world's first computer programmer.

Ada was the daughter of Lord Byron, a giant of romantic POETRY, but her own genius was mathematical. She was a true visionary who combined mathematics, logic, and imagination, predicting that machines might one day compose music and create art — more than a century before computers could do anything of the sort.

During World War Two, a BRITISH mathematician named Alan Turing helped change the course of history. At a secret facility called Bletchley Park, Turing and his team worked to break the codes produced by the German Enigma machine, which protected the enemy's most important military SECRETS.

Turing was a brilliant thinker who loved PUZZLES, and his WARTIME code-breaking is believed to have shortened the war by years and saved countless lives. He is often called the father of computer science, having imagined a theoretical computing device — now called a Turing machine — long before modern computers existed.

In 1945, one of the world's first general-purpose electronic computers was switched on: ENIAC. It was an ELECTRIC giant that filled an entire room, weighed about 30 tons, and contained thousands of glowing VACUUM tubes. Programming it meant physically rewiring the machine by hand — a very long way from typing on a keyboard.

One of the era's brightest pioneers was Grace Hopper. According to a famous story, when her team found a real moth stuck inside a MASSIVE computer and causing it to fail, they taped the insect into their logbook. Ever since, removing errors and INSECTS from programs has been called 'debugging'. Early computers were enormous, temperamental, and absolutely revolutionary.

Early programmers had to write in machine code — long strings of numbers that computers understood but humans found almost impossible to read. Then came a breakthrough: high-level programming languages. In 1957, a language called Fortran was created for scientific and mathematical work, letting people write instructions that looked much closer to human language.

Two years later, in 1959, Cobol arrived for business computing. These languages were difficult to build but laid the foundations of MODERN programming, because a special program called a compiler could translate the human-friendly code into the BINARY that machines actually run. Each new COMMAND brought computers closer to ordinary people, even if the underlying ideas remained genuinely COMPLEX.

By the 1970s, computers were shrinking from room-sized giants into machines that could sit on a desk at home. In 1975, two young programmers named Bill Gates and Paul Allen FOUNDED a company called Microsoft. A year later, in 1976, Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak started Apple, famously working out of a GARAGE.

A friendly programming language called BASIC made it possible for ordinary people — including curious teenagers — to write their own programs. Suddenly the computer was not just a tool for scientists and the military. It was affordable, it could fit on a DESKTOP, and the home computer boom turned a niche hobby into a worldwide STARTUP gold rush.

The final great leap was connecting computers together. In 1989, a British scientist named Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web while working at a research lab in Switzerland, creating a way for information to be linked and shared across a global NETWORK. Soon anyone with a web BROWSER could explore a vast and growing DIGITAL universe.

Modern programming then exploded. Free 'open-source' software, which anyone may use and improve, became essential, and friendly languages like Python and JavaScript let millions of people build almost anything. Today, code runs your phone, your car, and very possibly your toaster — proof that what began with a single WEBSITE has reshaped nearly every corner of life.
